## Recap: The Pipeline, Stage Two

Week 1's opening story: a manager at "StreamBase" hands you a pipeline diagram with six stages and
asks you to build it. Modules 1 and 2 built everything *underneath* that diagram — threads
(Module 1), and how separate machines talk to each other at all (Module 2). Starting today, we
build the diagram itself, one stage at a time.

```
ratings.csv + movies.csv   ← too big for one machine — today's whole problem
        ↓  hdfs dfs -put
      HDFS                  ← Modules 3: the next two weeks live here
        ↓  %%spark
    Apache Spark             (Module 4)
        ↓
     MongoDB                 (Module 5)
        ↓
    Flask API + Dashboard    (Module 6)
```

**Today's question, stage one:** before we can even talk about storing a file across many
machines, why does a file need that at all — why isn't one machine enough?

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Just re-anchor Week 1's bookmark slide — don't redraw the whole six-stage
diagram from memory, just enough to point at HDFS and say "that's where we are now."
:::

---

## Recap: Why One Machine Isn't Enough

Week 1 already did this arithmetic once — the StreamBase manager's ask was 80 billion events.
Quick replay:

- A laptop with 16 GB of RAM holds roughly **200 million integers** in memory at once.
- 80 billion rows is **400× that** — you'd need on the order of 400 machines just to *store* it,
  before any processing starts.
- Processing 80 billion rows sequentially, one machine, one core, at a generous 1 million
  rows/second, takes **over 22 hours** — for one pass over the data, one time.

That arithmetic is the entire justification for everything in this module: storage has to spread
across machines (HDFS), and so does the processing (MapReduce).

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** This is a recap, not a new derivation — if a student asks "wait, why 200
million integers," that's a Week 1 detail (4 bytes/int, 16 GB ÷ 4 bytes), not worth re-deriving
here. Move on.
:::

---

## Naming It: The Three Vs

Three vignettes from Week 1 were all "big data" problems — today they get a shared vocabulary:

| The "V" | What it means | The Week 1 vignette |
|---|---|---|
| **Volume** | The sheer amount of data exceeds one machine's storage | Google's web index — billions of pages, far more text than one machine could even read through |
| **Velocity** | New data arrives faster than one machine can keep up | Amazon's Black Friday — thousands of orders per second, all touching the same inventory data |
| **Variety** | The data isn't one clean, uniform shape | Netflix's recommendation signals — ratings, watches, pauses, skips, even hover time, all mixed together |

**Big data** = data that's too big, too fast-arriving, or too messily-shaped (often all three) for
one machine to handle alone.

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)

dwarfed by a large stack of stacked-disk icons on the right, with a "≠" or size-mismatch cue
between them. **Velocity:** a stopwatch icon with a fast-moving stream of small envelope/event
icons flowing into a funnel that's visibly overflowing. **Variety:** a cluster of differently
shaped icons — a spreadsheet grid, a photo, a speech-bubble, a raw text scroll — piled together
under one label, contrasted with a single neat table icon labeled "what one database table
expects." Caption under all three: "Too much. Too fast. Too messy — for one machine, one shape."
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Reusing Week 1's exact three vignettes is deliberate — the goal is precise

## Batch Processing: Meal-Prep, Not À La Carte

Once data is big in one of these ways, there are two general strategies for processing it:
handle each new piece of data the instant it arrives (**streaming** — out of scope this course), or
collect a pile of it and process the whole pile at once (**batch processing** — this module and
Module 4).

- **Kitchen picture:** a meal-prep Sunday, where a kitchen cooks a whole week's worth of a dish in
  one big batch, versus a restaurant cooking one dish fresh the instant each order comes in.
  Batch processing is the meal-prep Sunday: collect first, process the whole pile together.
- Classic real example: process yesterday's entire log file overnight, have results ready by
  morning — nobody needs the answer in the next 10 milliseconds, so batching the whole day's data
  together is simpler and more efficient than reacting to each log line individually.
- **MapReduce** (Google, 2004 — the paper from Week 1's Google vignette) is the framework that
  made batch processing on thousands of machines practical and programmable. You're about to
  invent a version of it yourself.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Keep this brief — it exists to set up "batch" as the vocabulary word for what
the activity is about to do, not to teach streaming as a topic (it isn't covered this course).
:::

## Today: Become the Cluster

For the rest of this session, no more slides about big data — you're going to **become** a small
distributed system and solve a real batch-processing problem with your own bodies, before any
formal vocabulary shows up.

- You'll work in **clusters of 3** — each of you is a separate "machine," sitting at a separate
  desk, not next to each other.
- Each of you gets a slice of a dataset — nobody sees the whole thing.
- Your cluster's job: combine your three slices into one correct answer, in as little time as
  possible, with your teammates spending as little time standing around waiting as possible.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Say explicitly: "I'm not going to tell you the algorithm. Figure one out, then
we'll name what you did." The entire value of the activity depends on not front-loading the
strategy.
:::

---

## Activity Setup

- Desks for each cluster of 3 are **spread apart** — corners of the room, not adjacent. Leaving
  your desk to check in with a teammate costs a real walk, not a whisper.
- Each cluster gets its own shuffled deck (or set of order strips) split three ways — one pile per
  student. Nobody's pile is sorted; your slice is a random mix of everything.
- **The rule that makes this interesting:** every trip you make to a teammate's desk costs time,
  and whoever you leave behind is sitting idle until you're back. A good cluster finishes fast
  *and* keeps everyone busy — not just one person doing all the walking while two people watch.

::: {.callout-note}

## Round 2: Minimize Trips, Minimize Waiting

Same task, a **fresh** dataset (new shuffled deck, or Set B's strips) — same three teammates.

**The challenge:** redesign your cluster's strategy, as a team, before you touch a single card or
strip. Your new strategy should try to minimize both:

1. **Trips** — how many times anyone leaves their desk
2. **Idle time** — how long anyone sits around waiting on a teammate

Take 2–3 minutes to plan out loud as a cluster. Then go, and track your trip count and time again.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 8 min (2–3 min planning + ~5 min execution).** If a cluster is stuck during planning,
the one hint to offer verbally (not written on this slide) is: "What if only one of you is
responsible for each suit / each menu item?" Let clusters that don't need the hint discover it
themselves — the discovery is the point.
:::

## Debrief: Naming What You Just Invented

Compare Round 2's trip count and time to Round 1's, cluster by cluster. Most clusters converge on
something like: each person first sorts and tallies *their own* pile alone at their desk — no
walking yet — then only a small written tally, not the raw pile, travels to whichever teammate
"owns" that suit or item.

| What your cluster just did | The real term (Wednesday gives you the details) |
|---|---|
| Each of you sorting/tallying your own pile, alone at your desk | **Map** — parallel, zero travel cost |
| Writing a small tally instead of carrying the raw pile | The instinct behind a real optimization Hadoop/Spark actually use |
| Carrying a tally to the one teammate who "owns" that key | **Shuffle** — the only phase that costs a physical trip |
| That teammate summing everything handed to them | **Reduce** |
| Sitting and waiting on a teammate's tally before you could finish | Exactly why a real job can bottleneck on its slowest worker |

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 6 min.** This table is the entire point of the session — don't rush it. If a cluster's
best strategy still didn't fully separate "map" from "shuffle," that's fine; name the ideal
strategy explicitly here even if no cluster found it on their own. Wednesday's opener re-reads this
exact table before introducing any code.
:::

## Meet Map, Shuffle, Reduce

**MapReduce** is a programming pattern for processing a big dataset by splitting it into pieces,
processing each piece independently, then combining the results — exactly what your cluster did
Monday, generalized to any number of "machines" and any counting problem, not just suits or menu
items.

```
Input data (split across N machines/files)
         ↓
    Map    — each machine processes only its own piece, in parallel
         ↓
  Shuffle/Sort — the framework groups everyone's output by key
         ↓
   Reduce — one machine per key combines that key's values into a final answer
         ↓
      Output
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)
Reuse Monday's kitchen-branch icon language. Three small "branch" icons on the left, each with its
own input pile, feeding downward arrows into a "Map" band where each branch is shown tallying its
own pile independently (no arrows *between* branches at this stage). Below that, a "Shuffle" band
where arrows converge from all three branches toward per-key collection points (e.g., one arrow
bundle labeled "♠" converging on one point, another labeled "♥" converging elsewhere) — these are
the only diagonal/crossing arrows in the whole diagram, visually marking this as the one phase that

value. Caption: "Same shape as Monday — just relabeled."
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Point at each band and ask "what did this look like in your cluster on Monday?"

## The Map Phase: One Record In, Zero or More Pairs Out

A **map function** takes one input record and emits **(key, value)** pairs — nothing more.

```
map(record):
    ... extract whatever matters from this one record ...
    emit(key, value)
```

Two examples of the same pattern, different data:

| Problem | What `map()` emits |
|---|---|
| Count words in a line of text | `emit(word, 1)` for every word in the line |
| Total sales per region, given `region, productID, saleAmount` records | `emit(region, saleAmount)` |

Notice what's the same in both: **one input record in, one small (key, value) pair out** — the
mapper never looks at any other record, and never talks to any other machine. Exactly like your
cluster tallying your own pile alone, Monday.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Think about it
A log file has one line per web request: `timestamp, userID, status_code`. You want to count how
many requests resulted in each status code (200, 404, 500, ...). What should `map()` emit?
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Callout answer: `emit(status_code, 1)` — structurally identical to word count
and the sales example, just a different field extracted. The point of showing three problems with
the same shape is pattern transfer, since Lab 4 and CP3 both hand students a *new* extraction
problem (email domains) they need to recognize as this same pattern.
:::

---

## The Shuffle/Sort Phase: The Framework's Job

After every machine finishes its map phase, all the emitted (key, value) pairs need to end up
grouped by key — every value for `"gmail.com"` in one place, every value for `"yahoo.com"` in
another — **regardless of which machine originally emitted them.**

- This is exactly Monday's "carry your tally to whoever owns that key" step — except now it's the
  **framework** doing the carrying, across a real network, not a student walking across a room.
- **You never write this step yourself.** Hadoop and Spark both do shuffle/sort automatically —
  it's the one phase of MapReduce with no function you implement.
- It's also the one phase that costs real network transfer — same as Monday, where trips were the
  only real cost. Map and Reduce, like your cluster's own tallying and summing, happen locally.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Emphasize "you never write this step" explicitly — CP3 only asks students to
write map-phase output precisely because shuffle and reduce's mechanics are the framework's job,
not something to hand-code.
:::

---

## The Reduce Phase: Combine Each Group Into One Answer

A **reduce function** receives one key and the full list of values shuffled to it, and produces
one final result for that key.

```
reduce(key, values):
    total = sum(values)
    emit(key, total)
```

- This runs once **per key**, on whichever machine the shuffle phase sent that key's values to —
  the same role as the one teammate on Monday who "owned" a suit or menu item and summed everything
  handed to them.
- Reduce doesn't have to mean "sum" — it could compute a maximum, an average, a count of distinct
  values, anything that combines a list into one answer. Summing is just today's example.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Keep this brief — it's the shortest of the three phase slides because it's the
most intuitive once Map and Shuffle are solid.
:::

---

## Word Count Walkthrough

The classic "Hello World" of MapReduce — structurally identical to Monday's activity, just
counting words instead of suits or menu items.

**Input:**
```
the quick brown fox
the fox jumped over the lazy dog
```

**Map phase** (one mapper per line):
```
(the,1) (quick,1) (brown,1) (fox,1)
(the,1) (fox,1) (jumped,1) (over,1) (the,1) (lazy,1) (dog,1)
```

**Shuffle/Sort** (grouped by key — the framework's work, not yours):
```
(brown,[1])  (dog,[1])  (fox,[1,1])  (jumped,[1])
(lazy,[1])   (over,[1]) (quick,[1])  (the,[1,1,1])
```

**Reduce phase** (sum each list):
```
(brown,1) (dog,1) (fox,2) (jumped,1) (lazy,1) (over,1) (quick,1) (the,3)
```

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Walk this top to bottom, pointing explicitly at which line is Map, which is
Shuffle, which is Reduce — this is the exact shape CP3 and Lab 4's email-domain problem reuse.
:::

---

## Why This Scales

Module 2 put it this way: *"a distributed system grows by adding more machines, not by buying an
impossibly bigger one."* That's called **scaling out** (add more machines) as opposed to
**scaling up** (buy one bigger machine) — MapReduce is the mechanism that makes scaling out
actually work for processing, not just storage.

- **Map tasks run in parallel**, one per input chunk — on a real cluster, ideally on the same
  machine that already holds that chunk of data. This is called **data locality**: compute goes
  *to* the data, not data to the compute. Kitchen picture: send the recipe to the branch that
  already has the ingredients, don't ship the ingredients to one central kitchen.
- **Reduce tasks also run in parallel**, one per key (or range of keys).
- **Only shuffle moves data across the network** — exactly the one phase that cost a trip on
  Monday. Everything else happens locally, at the same time, on every machine.
- Adding a 21st machine to a MapReduce cluster doesn't require rewriting `map()` or `reduce()` —
  it just means one more machine's worth of chunks processed in parallel. That's what "scaling
  out" buys you: capacity grows by adding machines, with the same code.

::: {.callout-important}
This is the same instinct your best cluster found in Round 2: move the small thing (a tally), not
the big thing (the raw pile). Data locality is that same idea, one level up — don't move the raw
data to the computation, move the (tiny, by comparison) computation to the data.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** The callout is the payoff of the whole activity — say explicitly that "data
locality" is the formal name for the exact efficiency idea their best Round 2 strategy already
discovered. The scale-up/scale-out distinction isn't tested by any checkpoint, quiz, or exam — it's
here only so the slide's own title ("scales") is earned by a definition rather than assumed. Don't
spend more than a sentence on it.
:::

---

## What the Framework Handles For You

Beyond running Map, Shuffle, and Reduce, Hadoop and Spark both handle a list of things you never
have to code yourself:

- **Task scheduling** — deciding which machine runs which chunk
- **Fault tolerance** — if a machine dies mid-job, its work gets reassigned and re-run elsewhere
- **Retries** — a failed task is retried automatically, not left broken
- **Progress tracking** — reporting how much of the job is done

You write `map()` and `reduce()`. The framework does everything else — a big part of why MapReduce
was such a breakthrough in 2004.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 2 min.** Keep brief — this is context for *why* the abstraction is valuable, not testable
detail.
:::

## Recap: From "How" to "Where"

Monday and Wednesday gave you MapReduce — the *program* that processes big data, split into Map,
Shuffle, and Reduce. But every one of those tasks has to run **somewhere**, reading a file that has
to **live somewhere**. Today: the file system that stores it (HDFS), and the software that decides
which machine runs which task (YARN) — the two real pieces underneath what Lab 4 only simulated in
local mode, and what Lab 5 runs for real this Friday.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Say explicitly: "Lab 4 ran without HDFS or YARN at all — that was deliberate,
so you could focus on the Mapper/Reducer code first. Today fills in the two pieces Lab 4 skipped."
:::

## Why Not Just a Regular File System?

A regular file system — the one on your laptop — lives on **one machine's one disk.**

- Its size is capped by that one disk, no matter how the rest of the data grows.
- If that one disk fails, everything on it is gone — no backup, nothing to fall back on.
- Only one machine can read it at a time — no way to spread the reading work across many machines.

**HDFS (Hadoop Distributed File System)** splits a file into pieces and spreads those pieces —
*plus duplicate copies* — across many machines' disks. The file can now be bigger than any single
disk, survives a disk failure, and can be read by many machines at once, in parallel. This is the
same **scaling out** idea from Wednesday — now applied to *storage*, not computation.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** One-sentence callback to Wednesday's scale-up/scale-out beat is enough — don't
re-derive it, just point at it: "same idea, different resource."
:::

---

## HDFS Blocks + Replication

- HDFS splits a file into fixed-size **blocks** (default 128 MB) — a large file becomes many
  blocks, scattered across many machines.
- Each block is stored on **3 machines**, not one (**replication factor = 3**).
- Kitchen picture: like stocking the same popular ingredient at 3 different branches, so one
  branch's fridge breaking down doesn't mean the whole company runs out of it.
- This is a **first, simpler taste** of the replication idea — Module 5 covers the full version,
  including *why* 3 copies, consistency between them, and what happens when one goes stale. For now:
  3 copies, automatic, so no single block is a single point of failure.

```
ratings.csv (say, 500 MB) → split into 4 blocks of ~128 MB each
  Block 1 → stored on Machine A, Machine C, Machine E
  Block 2 → stored on Machine B, Machine D, Machine A
  Block 3 → stored on Machine C, Machine E, Machine B
  Block 4 → stored on Machine D, Machine A, Machine C
```

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** The block-placement example is illustrative, not something to test — the point
is "different blocks can land on different machines, and each one is triplicated," not the exact
placement algorithm.
:::

---

## HDFS Architecture: The Address Book, Again

Module 2 gave you DNS: the internet's address book, translating a human-readable name into a
numeric address before your browser could even connect. HDFS has the **exact same shape of
problem** — given a filename, which machines actually hold its blocks?

- The **NameNode** is HDFS's version of that address book — it tracks which blocks belong to which
  file, and which machines hold each block. It does **not** store any of the actual file data
  itself.
- **DataNodes** are the machines that store the real block data.
- To read a file: the client asks the NameNode "where are this file's blocks?", the NameNode
  replies with a list of DataNode locations, and the client then reads the blocks **directly** from
  those DataNodes — the NameNode itself never touches the actual data.

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)
A client icon on the left. An arrow labeled "1. Where are ratings.csv's blocks?" pointing to a
central "NameNode" icon (drawn like an address-book/directory icon, visually matching Module 2's
DNS diagram style). A return arrow labeled "2. Blocks 1–4 are on Machines A, B, C..." pointing back
to the client. Then separate direct arrows labeled "3. Read block data" from the client straight to
3–4 "DataNode" icons (plain server/disk icons) — these arrows should visually bypass the NameNode
entirely, making clear the NameNode only answers the lookup, it doesn't relay any data itself.
Caption: "Same shape as DNS: ask the address book, then go straight to the real thing."
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** The "NameNode never touches the actual data" point is the one most worth
stating explicitly and slowly — it's the detail students most often get backwards, assuming the
NameNode is a relay rather than a lookup service.
:::

## HDFS Commands Demo

```
hdfs dfs -put ratings.csv /user/alice/    # upload: local file → HDFS
hdfs dfs -ls /user/alice/                 # list files in an HDFS directory
hdfs dfs -cat /user/alice/ratings.csv     # read a file's contents
hdfs dfs -get /user/alice/ratings.csv .   # download: HDFS → local file
```

- `-put` and `-get` are opposites: local-to-HDFS, and HDFS-to-local.
- `-ls` and `-cat` mirror the everyday Unix commands you already know, just pointed at HDFS instead
  of your local disk.
- This `-put` command is not a hypothetical — it's the literal first step of Week 1's Pipeline
  diagram, and the exact command Lab 10 has you run on `ratings.csv` and `movies.csv` for the
  capstone.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 5 min.** Actually run these four commands live against the classroom cluster if
possible, on a small throwaway file — seeing real output (a real file listing, real file contents)
lands better than reading the commands off a slide.
:::

---

## HDFS Design Principles

- **Write once, read many** — files aren't modified after writing; you write a file once, then
  only ever read it (or replace it entirely) afterward.
- **Data locality** — the same idea from Wednesday: MapReduce runs map tasks on the same machine
  that already holds the data block being processed.
- **Fault tolerance** — if a DataNode fails, its blocks are automatically re-replicated elsewhere
  from the remaining copies, restoring the replication factor of 3.
- **Not good for:** small files (overhead per file is high), low-latency access (built for
  throughput, not speed-of-single-lookup), or random writes (write-once-read-many, remember).

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** HDFS was designed for exactly the workload MapReduce produces — large,
sequential reads of immutable files. It's a poor choice for transactional workloads (that's what
Module 5's databases are for) — worth saying explicitly, since students may otherwise wonder why
the capstone uses *both* HDFS and MongoDB instead of just one.
:::

---

## YARN: Who Actually Runs the Job?

HDFS answers "where does the data live." **YARN** (Yet Another Resource Negotiator) answers "which
machine actually runs each Map or Reduce task, and who's keeping track?"

- **ResourceManager** — the whole branch network's dispatcher: one per cluster, deciding which
  worker machine handles a newly submitted job.
- **NodeManager** — each branch's own on-site manager: one per worker machine, actually running
  whatever tasks get assigned to that machine.
- **ApplicationMaster** — a coordinator dispatched specifically for **one job**: tracks that job's
  progress across whichever workers are running its tasks. One ApplicationMaster per job, not one
  for the whole cluster.

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagram to add later (Excalidraw / pyxcd / draw.io)

icon at the top. The ResourceManager fans out to 3 "NodeManager" icons, one per worker machine,
each drawn next to a small server/disk icon labeled "runs Map/Reduce tasks here." Keep this
diagram visually separate from the HDFS NameNode/DataNode diagram two slides back — same three
worker machines can appear in both, but the arrows and roles are different, and drawing them as one
combined diagram is exactly the confusion this split is meant to avoid.
:::

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 4 min.** Keep this the lightest new-content slide of the session — YARN internals aren't

attached to what's actually happening, not to be memorized role-by-role.
:::

## A MapReduce Job in Practice

The output directory of a completed Hadoop MapReduce job:

```
/output/
  _SUCCESS          ← empty file, signals the job completed successfully
  part-r-00000      ← actual output (one file per reducer)
  part-r-00001      ← (if 2 reducers were used)
```

- **Never overwrite** an existing output directory — Hadoop refuses, specifically to prevent
  accidental data loss. You'll see this exact error in Lab 5 if you forget to clean up first.
- Delete it yourself before re-running: `hdfs dfs -rm -r /output`

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** This is a direct preview of Lab 5's Task 3, Question 3 — say plainly that
they'll hit this refusal-to-overwrite behavior themselves on Friday, so it isn't a surprise.
:::

---

## From MapReduce to Spark

MapReduce already gets you scaling out for processing — but it has real limitations:

- Every job writes its intermediate results to **disk**, even between steps of the same
  pipeline — slow for anything iterative.
- The Mapper/Reducer API is low-level and verbose — hard to express a multi-step pipeline cleanly.
- No support for interactive, ask-a-question-and-wait-seconds-for-an-answer queries.

**Spark** (2009, Berkeley AMPLab) keeps intermediate data **in memory** instead of writing it to
disk between steps — 10–100× faster for iterative workloads. Same scaling-out idea as MapReduce;
Module 4 is about doing it faster.

::: {.notes}
**Timing: 3 min.** Keep the framing "same idea, faster mechanism" rather than "MapReduce is
obsolete" — Hadoop/HDFS is still the storage layer under Spark in this course's own pipeline.
:::

## Module 3 Summary

| Concept | Key idea |
|---|---|
| Big Data | Volume/velocity/variety that exceeds one machine |
| Map phase | Transform each record → (key, value) pairs, runs in parallel |
| Shuffle/Sort | Framework groups all pairs by key — no programmer work |
| Reduce phase | Aggregate values for each key → final output |
| Scaling out | Add more machines, same code — vs. scaling up (one bigger machine) |
| HDFS | Distributed file system: blocks + replication (×3) + NameNode/DataNode |
| YARN | Schedules and runs jobs across the cluster: ResourceManager/NodeManager/ApplicationMaster |

**Connects to:** Lab 4, Lab 5, Checkpoint 3, Quiz 3, Midterm Q25–Q35
